tagline.text: Pink coral-sand beach and protected seascape off Zamboanga

location.label: Location
location.text: An island in the Basilan Strait south of Zamboanga City, reached by boat from the Paseo del Mar jetty

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱500–1,500 (per person when the boat fare is shared; Manila airfare not included)

children.text: Great Santa Cruz Island is a small island about 4 km south of downtown Zamboanga, known for a beach whose white sand is tinted pink by crushed red coral. The boat from the city jetty takes about 15 minutes, and because the island is a protected seascape, visitors must follow its rules.
Great Santa Cruz Island is a small inhabited island in the Basilan Strait, south of Zamboanga City at the western tip of Mindanao. According to Wikipedia it lies about
4 km
south of downtown, and measures roughly
2.6 km
long and
1.5 km
wide, with a coastline of about
6.6 km
. It is small enough to walk around, and because it is so close to the city it is the first sea outing most visitors to Zamboanga think of.

The island is famous for the color of its sand. Fragments of red organ pipe coral, ground down by the surf, mix with white sand and give part of the beach a pink tint. Wikipedia calls it one of the few pink-sand beaches in the world and the only one in Asia, and notes that National Geographic included it among its "21 Best Beaches in the World" in 2017. The intensity of the pink changes with weather, tide, and light, so rather than expecting the vivid pink of photos, go with the idea of finding red coral fragments scattered among the grains of sand.

The island is part of the Great and Little Santa Cruz Islands Protected Landscape and Seascape. The protected area was established on April 23, 2000, under Proclamation No. 271 and covers about 1,877 hectares. Wikipedia explains that illegal coral mining in the past destroyed most of the reefs, leaving only dead skeletons, and that the city government is pursuing rehabilitation and ecotourism development. It is therefore better understood as a place to quietly see a protected coast and its sand than as a destination for spectacular coral diving.

The Sama-Bajau live on the island, and tourism reportedly began in the 1970s and early 1980s, when German, Japanese, and Italian travelers started to visit. Nearby Little Santa Cruz Island belongs to the same protected area and is described by Wikivoyage as having white sand. Travel information changes with local conditions, so check the latest notices from the city tourism office before you go.
Crushed red organ pipe coral mixes with white sand and gives the beach a pink tint. Taking sand, shells, or coral away is prohibited by the rules, so keep it to photos and memories.

You can sign up at the Paseo del Mar terminal for a boat tour through the mangroves. Per Wikivoyage it is

You can try rowing a traditional sailboat, the vinta. Wikivoyage lists it at

Before going to the island you attend a short briefing from tourism and environment staff. Single-use plastic and PET bottles are prohibited, so bring a reusable bottle.
Boats to the island leave from the Paseo del Mar jetty in the city. It is also the reclaimed esplanade that wraps Fort Pilar on the sea side, so it is a pleasant walk before or after your boat.

blocks.title: Life in a small island village

children.text: Sama-Bajau people live on the island. Their homes and living spaces are not tourist attractions but their daily lives, so ask permission before taking photos.
The island is only about
4 km
from the city, so it pairs well with Fort Pilar and Paseo del Mar in the afternoon. According to Wikipedia, the city is also a port town where a customs port was established in 1831.

items.title: Full-day plan
items.subtitle: Combining the island and the city's heritage

children.text: Take the island boat and spend about
2 hours
at the beach and nearby routes.
Return to the city for lunch. Zamboanga is a city where Chavacano, a Spanish-based creole, is spoken, and its signature seafood is curacha.
Walk to Fort Pilar. According to Wikivoyage, entry to the fort is free and candles cost
Finish by watching the sunset at Paseo del Mar.
According to Wikivoyage, PAL Express and Cebu Pacific fly from Manila to Zamboanga. Fares and schedules vary a lot by season, so check the airline apps.
You arrive at Zamboanga International Airport (ZAM) and take a taxi or tricycle to the city.
Wikivoyage says 2GO runs a ferry from Manila about once a week via Dipolog and Dumaguete. The voyage can take a long time, so allow plenty of time in your schedule.
A Ceres bus route is said to run from Manila via several Visayan cities. Confirm locally.

items.title: From the city to the island

children.text: The boat leaves from the Paseo del Mar jetty and takes about
15 minutes
one way.
Before departure, sign up for a boat at the city tourism office and attend the briefing.
Jeepneys are plentiful, but their routes are not clearly marked, so ask the driver.
Tricycle fares start at about
, and taxis are said to be scarce outside malls and the airport.
According to Wikivoyage, Zamboanga's dry season runs roughly from January to March, and the rest of the year is mostly rainy. Wikipedia's climate data show rainfall is lowest in February (about
55 mm
), highest from June to October, and peaks in October (about
197 mm
The island is open only during the daytime, and boats may not run when the sea is rough, so a clear dry-season morning is recommended. Daytime highs are around
all year, so bring sun protection.
According to Wikipedia's climate data, annual rainfall is about

, with around 113 rainy days a year and average humidity of about 81%. The city gets about 2,470 hours of sunshine a year, so the sun is strong on dry days. If you find it hard to pick a time, take the boat in the morning and spend the afternoon on city sights.

It is better to eat in the city. Wikivoyage introduces curacha (a large crab dish), satti, and baolo as local specialties, citing Alavar's Seafood House for curacha and Jimmy's Satti on Campaner Street for satti. Single-use plastic is not allowed on the island, so bring snacks in a container.

The common language of Zamboanga is Chavacano, which has Spanish roots, and Filipino and English are also widely used. The second most spoken language is Tausug. English is enough for shops and drivers, but saying thank you in Chavacano tends to get a warm response. For the island boat, a hotel near Paseo del Mar is the most convenient.

to
according to Wikivoyage, so leave in the morning.
The boat is a per-boat fare, so splitting it with companions lowers the cost per person.
Bring a reusable bottle and containers. Single-use plastic and PET bottles are prohibited.
Do not take sand, shells, or coral. This is prohibited by the rules.
Shade may be limited, so bring a hat, sunscreen, and water. Cottages can be rented on site.
The pink looks different depending on weather. Try taking photos on a clear morning when the sunlight is low.
Ask permission before taking photos in residents' living areas.
Safety information for Zamboanga changes often. Before you leave, check the travel advisory from your government and the latest local notices.

Wikivoyage says the city is generally safe but is not considered one of the safest cities in Mindanao, and that some international travel agencies advise against visiting. Check the latest information before your trip.
Watch for pickpockets in busy downtown areas.
Boats may not run when waves are high or the weather is bad. Check refund and rescheduling rules in advance.
The island is a protected area, so do not step on or collect coral. Wikipedia explains that illegal mining in the past killed much of the reef.
The fees and opening hours come from Wikivoyage and may change. Always confirm locally.

A 17th-century Spanish fort near the jetty where the island boats depart. According to Wikipedia, the Jesuit priest and engineer Melchor de Vera laid its cornerstone on June 23, 1635, which is also counted as the founding of Zamboanga. It was a defense against raids by Moro pirates and the Sulu and Maguindanao sultanates, and it was declared a National Cultural Treasure in 1973. Today it houses a branch of the National Museum and an outdoor shrine of Our Lady of the Pillar, and per Wikivoyage entry is free. It is about
10 minutes
away on foot.
A reclaimed esplanade with the boat jetty that wraps Fort Pilar on the sea side. It is a good place to watch the sunset.
